rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lexical discussion of al-ḥamd was already presented in the commentary on Sūrat al-Fātiḥah.
rows.anchor: was presented in the exegesis of S ūrah al-Fātiḥah.

rows.speaker: Idolaters of Arabia
rows.claim: The Arabian Idolaters acknowledged God as creator of the heavens, earth, darkness, and light.
rows.anchor: the Idolaters of Arabia regarded God to be the creator of the heavens and the earth as well of darkness and light.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their admission that God created everything makes their ascription of partners to Him inexplicable.
rows.anchor: when everything has been created by God, from where has the possibility of polytheism arisen?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opposing elements such as sky and earth, light and darkness, and cold and heat harmonize toward one purpose, pointing insightful people to one creator and intent.
rows.anchor: in the apparent conflict found in the opposing elements of nature, to fulfil a higher objective there exists tremendous harmony between them as well.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an repeatedly alludes to humanity’s creation from clay, exemplified by 32:7.
rows.anchor: The fact that human beings are made from clay is alluded to at a number of occasions in the Qur’ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clay origin of humans points to their humble beginnings and should prevent arrogance.
rows.anchor: First, at the trivial substance of creation of human beings. Thus, they should not become arrogant.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse’s focus is resurrection: God who first created humans from clay can recreate them, as the cited verses affirm.
rows.anchor: In the verse under discussion, the purpose is to allude to the latter reality.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ajal means “period”; ajalan musamman is used for individuals and nations in three senses: a person’s lifespan, the Day of Judgment, or a nation’s allotted existence.
rows.anchor: The word أﺟﻞmeans “period” and the term أﺟﻞ ﻣﺴﻤﻰ is used in the Qur’ ān with

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this verse, the first occurrence of ajal denotes each person’s lifespan and the second the appointed time of resurrection; 6:60 is another example of the first sense.
rows.anchor: The first instance refers to the time of life of every individual, while the second instance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A nation’s term follows moral laws, unlike an individual’s lifespan: faithful conduct can preserve it, and repentance before destruction can win it more time.
rows.anchor: the life of a nation is governed by moral laws: as long as a nation preserves its faith and character

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term translated as quibbling derives from a root meaning squeezing or pressing; here it describes polemical argument meant to cast doubt on an established truth.
rows.anchor: Here it refers to quibbling and polemical arguments given by a debater to create doubt in something which is

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the Quraysh admit that God made humans from clay and allotted each a lifespan, they have no rational ground to doubt His power to resurrect them at the time only He knows.
rows.anchor: He has fixed a time for this and only He has knowledge of this time.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh persist in debating a certain truth despite there being no room for doubt or discussion.
rows.anchor: This is a certain reality in which there is no possibility of any debate or discussion. However, the Quraysh are adamant on their quibbling.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone rules both the heavens and earth, as also stated in 43:84.
rows.anchor: It is further implied that the heavens and he earth do not have separate gods. He is the master of both and each is under His command.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heavens and earth’s sustained existence points to one divine intent; otherwise, they would have been destroyed.
rows.anchor: Had this not been the case, both would have been destroyed as is mentioned elsewhere in the Qur’ ān (21:22).

rows.speaker: Idolaters
rows.claim: Some Idolaters held that God delegated the earth’s governance to His workers because it was remote from His kingdom; Islahi rejects this view.
rows.anchor: This verse actually refutes a certain opinion of the Idolaters.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God directly governs both realms and needs no helper because He knows people’s intentions, words, and deeds.
rows.anchor: Such is His knowledge that He knows the intentions, words and deeds of people. Thus He does not need any helper in His kingdom.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Belief in the hereafter is essential; without it, worldly life becomes mere amusement.
rows.anchor: it is essential to believe in the hereafter because without this belief, this world is rendered into a place of amusement.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Idolaters’ belief that divine partners can secure forgiveness for their worshippers regardless of their deeds empties the hereafter of significance.
rows.anchor: the partners of God will be able to have all their worshippers – whatever deeds they committed – forgiven from God, as was claimed by the Idolaters

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The truth” denied by the disbelievers here means the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: The word “truth” here refers to the Qur’ ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They mocked the Qur’an because it warned them of punishment for rejecting the messenger.
rows.anchor: They were making fun of it because it was warning them of a punishment if they rejected the messenger.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: History supports the warning: no nation escaped punishment for rejecting a messenger, and the Quraysh should take heed; al-A‘rāf, its counterpart sūrah, gives details.
rows.anchor: No nation was spared from the punishment of denying a messenger and the Quraysh too must realize this.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Samāʾ can mean either “sky” or “clouds.”
rows.anchor: just as it means “sky.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word mudrāran is emphatic and means abundant rain and copious sustenance; it also appears in 11:52 and 71:11.
rows.anchor: carries exaggeration and emphasis in it and signifies abundant rain and copious sustenance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objections and demands answer the Quraysh’s earlier aversion to the Qur’an; even if met, they would invent new excuses because rejection stems from desire, not a lack of miracles.
rows.anchor: the reason of their not accepting it is that it is against their desires and not any lack of miracles shown to them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first response answers a demand from the People of the Book cited at 4:154, with a reply suited to them.
rows.anchor: answer to the demand of the People of the Book cited in their own words in verse 154 of Sūrah al-Nisā’.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next verse presents and answers the Quraysh’s second demand, the request for an angel to descend openly.
rows.anchor: The second verse mentions their second demand and its answer.
